title: The Somerton Man: Identified 74 Years Later?
parts: In nineteen forty eight, a man was found dead on a beach in Australia.
No wallet. No ID. Every tag cut out of his clothes.
Inside a hidden, stitched pocket, there was a scrap of paper. It said just one word: "ended."
For seventy four years, nobody could say who he was.
Then, in twenty twenty two, researchers said they finally had a name.
We will mark every claim here: documented, disputed, or no evidence found.
By the end, you will know exactly what was found on that beach, and what a strange code hidden inside a stolen book still hasn't told anyone.
You will meet the name researchers gave him in twenty twenty two.
And you will learn why, even with a name, the official case still is not closed.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, the beach.
December first, nineteen forty eight. Somerton Park, near Glenelg, South Australia.
A man was found propped against the sea wall, legs out, shoes neatly crossed.
People who had seen him the night before said he looked like he was just... asleep.
No wallet. No identification. Every clothing tag had been cut out, on purpose.
Documented, by the original police investigation.
The cause of death was never officially settled.
The pathologist at the time suspected poison, something like a sedative.
Two toxic substances were found in his body, digitalis and ouabain, but their names weren't made public for decades.
In the end, the original coroner could not determine an official cause of death. The case closed without a verdict.
In nineteen ninety four, a judge reviewed the case and said he believed it was digitalis. That's one man's opinion, decades later, not a new forensic finding.
Disputed. No poison was ever actually found in the body during the original autopsy.
Months after the body was found, police searched his clothing again.
Sewn into a hidden pocket, they found a tiny rolled scrap of paper.
Printed on it, two words in Persian: "Tamam Shud." It means "ended," or "finished."
That scrap had been torn from the last page of a rare book, a nineteen forty one New Zealand edition of a Persian poem called the Rubaiyat.
A man later handed police a matching copy of that exact book.
Documented. The paper and the book are real, physical evidence, confirmed under a microscope.
Inside the back cover of that book, something stranger.
Faint pencil marks: five lines of capital letters, one of them crossed out.
In nineteen seventy eight, Australian military codebreakers said a real answer might be impossible, the text could be too short, or not even a code at all.
Since then, researchers have proposed it's initials of words, or shorthand. One twenty fourteen analysis found no match at all.
No proposed answer has ever been accepted by authorities as definitive.
No evidence found. After nearly fifty years, nobody has cracked it in a way that's actually been confirmed.
And then, in twenty twenty two, a possible breakthrough.
Researchers Derek Abbott and Colleen Fitzpatrick said DNA pointed to a name: Carl Webb, an electrical engineer born in nineteen oh five.
The DNA came from hairs trapped in a plaster death mask made of his face, back in nineteen forty nine. Not from the body itself.
From that DNA, they built a family tree, reaching distant cousins, until they landed on Webb.
Police said they were, quote, cautiously optimistic. They did not confirm it.
Family photos surfaced. Divorce papers from nineteen fifty one described him as difficult, and sometimes violent.
One of the genealogists said she was, quote, one hundred percent convinced. An independent forensic scientist said she wasn't sure we would ever reach absolute certainty.
Disputed. This is a proposed identification from an independent research team, not a confirmation from police or a coroner.
And still, nobody has an official answer for why he died, or how he ended up on that beach.
In twenty twenty one, authorities exhumed the body, hoping for DNA straight from the remains this time, not from a mask.
That's a stronger kind of test than hair on plaster.
As of the most recent sources we could find, that comparison has not been made public.
South Australia police have called the case, quote, complex and ongoing.
Documented: this case has never been officially closed. Disputed: exactly where it stands right now.
Over the decades, people have floated spy theories, Cold War connections, secret codes tied to nearby weapons testing sites.
None of them have ever been backed by real evidence.
At least eight different people were "positively" identified as him back in nineteen forty nine. Every single one turned out to be wrong.
No evidence found, for every one of these.
So, what do we actually know?
The body, the hidden note, the book: documented. The cause of death, and the twenty twenty two identification: disputed. The code, and every spy theory: no evidence found.
A name is not the same thing as an answer.
So who was the Somerton Man?
Maybe Carl Webb. Maybe not, according to the people whose job it actually is to confirm it.
And that leaves one real question: if we can put a name to a man seventy four years later and still not know how or why he died, what else might we be wrong about calling "solved"?
